clue.text: Final course, perhaps, for dunce

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a creamy fruit pudding served as dessert
second meaning: a silly, stupid person

explanation.surface: A slow pupil faces a last lesson, perhaps a final course for the dunce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests study, but here it is a course of a meal; a gooseberry fool is a classic British dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a whipped fruit-and-cream pudding eaten last and a person lacking sense.

clue.text: Left in accommodation, a doctor recorded his cases

indicators.note: the letter for left is put inside the lodging word, as a guest is put up in rooms

parts.note: homes are places of accommodation
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A physician on holiday lodgings writes up his patient files.
explanation.walkthrough: Sherlock Holmes's cases were written up by his companion Dr Watson, so the whole second half is a descriptive definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Watson narrated the detective stories, so the detective is the man whose cases a doctor chronicled.

clue.text: Bear exactly 50% of ridicule

indicators.note: taking precisely half of a word means dropping the other half of its letters

parts.note: to pooh-pooh something is to dismiss it with scorn

explanation.surface: A bear seems to be the precise target of half of the mockery going round.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb pooh-pooh is two identical halves, so taking exactly half leaves one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnie-the-Pooh is the famous honey-loving bear of A. A. Milne's children's stories.

clue.text: Oval then Lord's welcoming new batsman initially

indicators.note: this word places one piece straight after the other in sequence

parts.note: an oval shape looks like the letter O

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a lord is a peer of the realm
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: At cricket, the Oval and then Lord's grounds greet a fresh batsman starting out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval and Lord's are London cricket grounds, which disguises the plain O and the lord as a peer.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the first batsmen in an innings are called openers, so one who bats initially fits.

clue.text: Case for moving leaves a head in trying situation

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, as something sits in a place

parts.note: a test is a trying situation
so much a head means so much each

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a packing case, leaving a head stuck in an awkward spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as a verb but belongs to the definition: the box was made for shipping tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea chest is a light wooden box built to ship tea and widely reused for packing when moving house.

clue.text: Person with chair, one piece of furniture that's useful

parts.note: a professor holds a university chair
Roman numeral one
a table is furniture

explanation.surface: Someone owning a chair and one more item of furniture finds it all handy.
explanation.walkthrough: A chair here is a professorship, not a seat, despite the furniture beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something profitable is beneficial or rewarding, which makes it useful in a broad sense.

clue.text: Red, for instance, in US leading commotion in state

indicators.note: being in the lead means coming first, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: American spelling of colour, of which red is an example
ado is fuss or commotion

explanation.surface: A Red agitator causes a stir somewhere in an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in US' signals the American spelling without the U.
explanation.definitionFit: Colorado is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Rocky Mountains.

clue.text: As it is, when reduced to symbol

definitions.text: As it is, when reduced to symbol

parts.note: surface reading: an everyday phrase meaning in the present state of affairs
setter's reading: the element whose chemical symbol is As

explanation.surface: Things stand just as they are, once boiled down to a sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is not a conjunction: it is a chemical symbol, and 'it' is the element it stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: The poisonous element number 33 is written As in the periodic table.

clue.text: Essay on American author's kind of literary work

indicators.note: one piece placed on another in an across clue follows it

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, American writer
to essay is to try or attempt

explanation.surface: A school essay about an American writer's style of literature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' looks like a noun for a composition, but it is the verb meaning attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetry is writing in verse, one of the main forms of literature.

clue.text: Beasts of burden bringing little back across area

indicators.note: bringing something back sends it the other way, so the word reads right to left
stretching across something means spanning it, so one piece goes either side of the other

parts.note: little means small
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Pack animals carry little loads back across a region.
explanation.definitionFit: Llamas are South American camelids used to carry loads in the Andes, so they are pack animals.

clue.text: Restrain worker heading strike

indicators.note: something heading another goes at its front, so this piece comes first

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker
to cuff is to strike with the hand

explanation.surface: Police restrain a labourer who is leading a walkout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action alongside the worker, but it means a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To handcuff someone is to lock their wrists together, physically restraining them.

clue.text: Tense reason to change nothing?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a grammatical tense, as in 'I have eaten'

definitions.note: read as a situation: the present being perfect
definitions.meaning: second meaning: if things now are flawless, there is nothing to alter

explanation.surface: A nervous person finds a motive for leaving everything as it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for anxious, but it is the grammar term; the second half is read literally, the present being perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: The grammatical tense formed with have plus a past participle, and the literal idea that the current moment is ideal.

clue.text: Narrative about old Conservative's moving deed

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a relation is an account or telling of events
O is the abbreviation for old
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A story about an old Tory's touching act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' suggests emotional, but it means changing place.
explanation.definitionFit: Relocation is the act of moving somewhere else, so it is a deed of moving.

clue.text: Quietly covering main part, carry on lawsuit

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece covering another sits on top of it

parts.note: p for piano, the musical instruction for quiet
the lead is the principal role

explanation.surface: A lawyer, softly covering the key section, presses on with a case.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'covering' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to argue a case in court, so it is to conduct a lawsuit.

clue.text: Start off car, young man, in gear

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of car
a lad is a young man

explanation.surface: A young driver gets the car going, in gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gear' suggests a car's gearbox, but it means clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clad means dressed, and to be in gear is to be wearing clothing.

clue.text: Belittle good-looker in revealing garment? Just the opposite

indicators.note: one piece placed inside another, then flipped by the closing phrase
this reverses which piece holds which, so the outer becomes inner

parts.note: a dish is an attractive person
a miniskirt, short and revealing

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at an attractive person in a skimpy outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says the beauty goes inside the garment, then 'Just the opposite' puts the garment inside the beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: To diminish someone is to make them seem smaller or less important, which is belittling them.

clue.text: Fellow holding tune, finally, for a song

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: a chap is a fellow

indicators.note: the final letter of the preceding word is the one kept

parts.note: last letter of tune

explanation.surface: A man humming the end of a melody gets something almost free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a song' is an idiom for very little money, despite the musical tune beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bought for a song is an idiom meaning bought at a very low price, so inexpensive.

clue.text: Under pressure, tell bishop, for example

indicators.note: in a down clue being under something means following it, so order is fixed

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
to relate is to tell

explanation.surface: Pushed hard, someone informs on a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly the telling sits under the pressure in the column, so 'Under pressure' fixes the order.
explanation.definitionFit: A prelate is a senior churchman, and a bishop is the standard example.

clue.text: Bit of brass neighbour returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so read the word backwards

parts.note: to abut is to border on, be neighbour to

explanation.surface: The family next door gave back a brass ornament they borrowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests metal or money, but it is the brass section of an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the largest brass instrument, one member of an orchestra's brass section.

clue.text: Things like this restricting pre-noon game, note, for some sportsmen

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so the following pieces sit inside the first

parts.note: this is a crossword clue, and these are clues
a.m. means before noon
bridge is a card game
B is a musical note

explanation.surface: Some sports teams get puzzles like this one that limit a morning match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Things like this' points at the clue itself. A Blue is an athlete who has represented Oxford or Cambridge against the other university.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambridge Blues are students awarded colours for representing their university in sport.

clue.text: English in recovery — are you sure?

indicators.note: one piece placed inside the other, as something sits in a place

parts.note: a rally is a recovery, as in prices
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English patient on the mend is asked whether they're certain.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole question, matched by the incredulous single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as a question, 'really?' expresses doubt or surprise, asking whether someone is certain.

clue.text: I'll be upset over small attacks on paper

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece lying over another stands above it
upset things are knocked into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone vows to be distressed by petty criticism in print.
explanation.definitionFit: Libels are false, damaging statements published in writing, so they are attacks made on paper.

clue.text: Normal colours

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a flag or banner carried by a regiment

explanation.walkthrough: 'Colours' here is a regiment's flag, not hues.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the usual level and the ensign carried into battle.

clue.text: Mild expletive that's used by Morse

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the long signal in Morse code

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse sticks to the gentlest of swear words.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse suggests the TV detective, but it is the telegraph code of dots and dashes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a genteel oath and the long element alongside the dot in telegraph code.

clue.text: Sudden attack from male concealed by some foliage?

indicators.note: something concealed by another is hidden within it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a bush, one bit of foliage
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A man hiding in the undergrowth springs out on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also hints at the scene: an ambusher lurks in the shrubs.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise attack launched from hiding.

clue.text: Not without reason, only partly believes an expert or trusts a nerd

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used, so the entry sits within them

parts.note: the letters run across the word boundaries
surface padding that offers a second hiding place for the same four letters

explanation.surface: Someone half-believes a specialist, or trusts a geek.
explanation.walkthrough: The same letters also run through 'trusts a nerd', so either phrase serves.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sane has their reason, so they are not lacking it, a double negative for rational.

clue.text: Roman magistrate imprisoned people, primarily upholding law

parts.note: cons are convicts

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the first letters are kept

parts.note: first letters of upholding and law

explanation.surface: A Roman official jails people, first and foremost upholding the law.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome two consuls were elected each year as the chief magistrates of the republic.

clue.text: Clinching time inside for criminal activity

indicators.note: this word places one piece within the other

parts.note: sealing a deal clinches it
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A villain gets locked up for a spell inside for his crimes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time inside' suggests a prison sentence, but it is just a T placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealing is theft, a common form of crime.
